title: Homeowner may disclose excessive personal and household details during registration and device enrollment
description: During account registration and enrollment of cameras/sensors, the homeowner may provide more personal data than is necessary, such as full identity details, precise home characteristics, room names, or device labels that reveal intimate household activities. The act of sharing this data from the source creates a disclosure risk.
assumptions: Registration and enrollment collect user identity/account data plus device metadata such as names, locations, and capabilities.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Registration and enrollment traffic can link the homeowner to a specific smart-home installation
description: Data in transit may contain stable identifiers, account identifiers, device serial numbers, MAC addresses, or network metadata that allow observers or intermediaries to link multiple enrollment events to the same homeowner and household over time.
assumptions: The flow carries account and device identifiers during setup, and some network or protocol metadata may be observable in transit.
uncertainty_note: Exact identifiers present on the wire are not specified; applicability depends on protocol and transport protections.

title: Enrollment messages may identify the homeowner or household if intercepted
description: Registration and device-enrollment traffic may directly or indirectly identify the homeowner or their residence through names, email addresses, phone numbers, addresses, device identifiers, or other unique setup data transmitted on this flow.
assumptions: The flow includes account-registration attributes and device identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Likelihood depends on whether strong transport encryption and minimization are used.

title: Home Hub may store or process more registration and device data than necessary
description: On receipt of registration and enrollment data, the Home Hub may retain excessive personal information or detailed device metadata, such as room assignments, camera names, or historical enrollment details, beyond what is needed to provide the service. This creates a disclosure threat at the destination.
assumptions: The Home Hub persists account and device-enrollment information locally or in associated management components.
uncertainty_note: Specific retention behavior is not described; threat is grounded in common onboarding implementations.

title: Homeowner may be unaware of how registration and enrollment data will be used
description: The Home Hub may collect account and device-enrollment data without making it sufficiently clear how the data will be used, retained, combined, or shared, leaving the homeowner insufficiently informed at the point of collection.
assumptions: Privacy notices or just-in-time explanations may be absent or incomplete during setup.
uncertainty_note: Applies if setup UX lacks clear notice; the flow description alone does not confirm this.

title: Registration and enrollment may proceed without valid, specific consent for personal and household data processing
description: The Home Hub may accept registration and device-enrollment data and begin processing personal and household information without obtaining consent that is freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous where such consent is required. This is especially relevant if camera/sensor metadata reveals behavior inside the home.
assumptions: Consent is a relevant legal basis for at least some setup-related processing or optional features.
uncertainty_note: Legal basis may alternatively be contract or legitimate interests for core setup; applicability depends on jurisdiction and processing purpose.

title: Observation of unlock-code entry can reveal guest participation
description: The existence and timing of the Guest User's communication with the Home Hub can be observed at the interface or nearby, allowing an observer to infer that a guest is currently attempting to access the home, even without learning the code itself.
assumptions: Assumes the code entry interaction is observable through the hub UI, keypad activity, or network signaling visible to an observer.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement from LINDDUN Detecting categories; the retrieved context confirms Detecting applicability but not the exact node numbering.

title: Home Hub may identify the guest through the temporary access code
description: If each temporary access code is unique per guest or booking, the Home Hub can identify or single out the guest when receiving the code, linking the interaction to a specific individual or household visitor.
assumptions: Assumes temporary codes are uniquely assigned or otherwise attributable to a particular guest.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; applicability depends on whether codes are unique per guest.

title: Temporary access code can link guest access events across time
description: When the Home Hub stores or processes the same temporary code across multiple unlock attempts, it may link separate access events to the same guest, enabling reconstruction of visit patterns.
assumptions: Assumes the hub logs or otherwise retains code-related events over time.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; threat depends on retention or repeated use of the same code.

title: Guest may be unable to deny having used the temporary code
description: If the Home Hub records successful or failed code-entry events together with timestamps and code identifiers, those records may later be used as evidence that the guest attempted or obtained entry, reducing plausible deniability.
assumptions: Assumes the hub keeps audit or event logs tied to the temporary code.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; applicability depends on logging practices.

title: Guest may be unaware of logging and secondary use of code-entry data
description: The guest may not understand that entering a temporary access code at the Home Hub could trigger storage of timestamps, failed attempts, occupancy inferences, or onward sharing with other home-management components.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly inform guests about collection, retention, and downstream use of access-event data.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; this is a common unawareness risk at the receiving process.

title: Guest code entry may occur without meaningful consent or choice
description: A guest may have to provide the temporary access code to gain entry, without a practical opportunity to consent to associated personal-data processing such as event logging or profiling of presence.
assumptions: Assumes code entry is mandatory for access and privacy choices are not separately offered.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; applicability depends on the system's consent model and legal basis.

title: Sensor-event logging reveals occupants' behavior patterns
description: By writing detailed motion, door, and other sensor events to the log, the Home Hub creates a record from which presence, absence, routines, sleep/wake cycles, and room usage can be inferred.
assumptions: Event entries contain timestamps and sensor identifiers or locations.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement at a generic detectability/disclosure node because the retrieved context did not include detailed threat-tree ids.

title: Local event log can link multiple events to the same household or occupants
description: The Local Event Log aggregates repeated sensor events over time, enabling correlation of events to the same home, device set, and potentially specific occupants, which increases linkability across activities.
assumptions: The datastore retains identifiers such as device IDs, room labels, household ID, or stable timestamps.
uncertainty_note: Specific LINDDUN Pro subtree id may differ; using a generic linkability node based on standard LINDDUN reasoning.

title: Stored event history may identify residents or visitors
description: Even if individual sensor events seem low sensitivity, the accumulated local log can identify a household or particular individuals through unique movement patterns, occupancy schedules, or association with labeled devices/rooms.
assumptions: Logs are retained long enough and contain sufficiently granular timestamps or contextual labels.
uncertainty_note: Identification may be indirect and depends on log granularity and auxiliary knowledge.

title: Local event log enables inference of intimate household activities
description: The destination datastore stores fine-grained event sequences that can disclose sensitive facts such as when the home is empty, when occupants sleep, or unusual activity patterns.
assumptions: The log is accessible to local admins, support personnel, malware, or other components beyond the immediate event-processing purpose.
uncertainty_note: Using generic disclosure/detectability node due to missing detailed tree mapping in retrieved context.

title: Broad or indefinite local logging may exceed users' expectations
description: Persisting all motion/door/sensor events in a local datastore can be unexpected or insufficiently transparent to residents, creating a privacy threat if users are unaware of the extent, retention, or secondary uses of the log.
assumptions: Users are not clearly informed about local event retention and use.
uncertainty_note: This is an unawareness threat grounded in likely lack of transparency; applicability depends on product notices and UI.

title: Event-log retention or use may violate data-minimization and storage-limitation expectations
description: Storing detailed sensor events in the Local Event Log may be non-compliant if more data than necessary is retained, retained too long, or reused for purposes beyond operating the Home Hub.
assumptions: There is no strict retention limit, purpose limitation, or configurable deletion policy.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends on applicable policy/regulatory context and actual retention controls.

title: Excessive disclosure of recorded video clips by the Home Hub
description: The Home Hub may upload full recorded camera clips, potentially including bystanders, visitors, interiors, audio, timestamps, and other contextual details, even when only a subset is necessary for the intended service. The source's act of sharing rich footage to the cloud creates a disclosure risk.
assumptions: Assumes clips contain personal data and that not all uploaded content is strictly necessary for the intended cloud-storage purpose.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement for disclosure via over-collection/over-sharing; exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Linkability via upload metadata on the clip-transfer flow
description: Even if clip contents are protected, metadata on the upload flow—such as device identifiers, account identifiers, IP address, timing/frequency of uploads, clip sizes, and camera/source labels—can allow linking multiple uploads to the same household, device, or user over time.
assumptions: Assumes the transfer exposes or carries stable identifiers or observable metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact applicable sub-node may differ depending on whether protocol metadata, identifiers, or traffic analysis is in scope.

title: Identifiability of household or occupants from clip-transfer metadata
description: The upload flow may reveal who the data relates to through identifiers and network metadata, or through the clip payload itself if intercepted or otherwise observable in transit. This can make the household, residents, or visitors identifiable.
assumptions: Assumes uploads contain direct or indirect identifiers, or that traffic metadata can be associated with a known household/account.
uncertainty_note: Applies strongly if transport metadata or payload is accessible to intermediaries or observers; exact node id is approximate.

title: Disclosure through cloud-side access or secondary use of stored clips
description: Once received, Cloud Video Storage may expose clips to cloud operators, internal analytics, support personnel, third parties, or other unauthorized recipients, or use them beyond the user's expected storage purpose. The destination's storage and processing behavior creates the disclosure risk.
assumptions: Assumes cloud storage involves provider-side access paths or secondary processing beyond strictly isolated storage.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node is approximate; intended to capture recipient-side disclosure/oversharing or unauthorized access.

title: Unawareness about cloud retention and processing of uploaded clips
description: Individuals captured in the recordings—and possibly even the device owner—may be unaware that clips are uploaded to cloud storage, how long they are retained, who can access them, and for what additional purposes they may be processed.
assumptions: Assumes transparency notices or in-context indicators are incomplete for data subjects and/or the account holder.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; captures lack of transparency at the receiving/storage side.

title: Non-compliance risk from storing camera clips in the cloud without adequate legal/privacy controls
description: Uploading and storing home-camera clips in cloud storage may violate privacy obligations if the service lacks an appropriate legal basis, purpose limitation, data minimization, retention limits, cross-border safeguards, or data-subject rights handling. The destination's storage practices create the compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes the clips contain personal data and are subject to privacy regulation or contractual privacy commitments.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends heavily on jurisdiction and implementation details; node id is best-effort.

title: Repudiation of receipt or storage actions for uploaded clips
description: If Cloud Video Storage lacks adequate logging, receipts, or audit trails, the provider may be unable to prove when clips were received, stored, accessed, deleted, or shared. This undermines accountability for privacy-relevant handling of the uploaded footage.
assumptions: Assumes insufficient auditability or evidentiary records for storage lifecycle events.
uncertainty_note: Included as an accountability/privacy threat; exact sub-node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Inability to exercise deletion over uploaded cloud clips
description: After clips are uploaded, the cloud storage service may retain copies, backups, replicas, or derived data in ways that prevent timely deletion or full erasure when requested. This reduces the data subject's or owner's ability to control and dispose of the footage.
assumptions: Assumes cloud storage uses backups/replication or lacks robust deletion propagation.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; intended to capture loss of control over deletion/disposal at the destination.

title: Home Hub may disclose more motion-alert data than necessary to the backend
description: When forwarding a real-time motion alert, the Home Hub may include excessive personal data beyond what is strictly needed for alert handling, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, household identifiers, sensor metadata, or repeated/raw event details. This creates an avoidable disclosure from the source to another party in the system.
assumptions: Assumes the motion alert contains or can be linked to household occupancy/activity information and that some included fields may be unnecessary for backend processing.

title: Real-time motion-alert transmissions may enable linkage of events to a household or user over time
description: Even if payload contents are limited, repeated real-time alert messages and their metadata on this flow (timing, frequency, routing, persistent identifiers) can allow correlation of multiple events to the same home, device, or account. This can support building behavioral patterns such as occupancy routines.
assumptions: Assumes the flow uses stable identifiers or otherwise observable metadata that permits correlating multiple alerts over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include linkage subnodes for this flow.

title: Motion-alert metadata may identify a household or resident
description: The alert payload or transport metadata may contain direct or indirect identifiers, such as hub IDs, account IDs, network endpoints, or uniquely patterned event timing, that make the household or associated user identifiable on this flow.
assumptions: Assumes identifiers or sufficiently unique quasi-identifiers are present in the transmitted data or metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include identifiability subnodes.

title: Backend can infer sensitive occupancy patterns from received motion alerts
description: On receipt of real-time motion alerts, the mobile app backend can derive additional personal information not explicitly sent, such as presence at home, daily routines, sleep/wake cycles, or periods of absence. These inferences may exceed what users expect from simple alert forwarding.
assumptions: Assumes the backend stores or analyzes alert history rather than treating each alert ephemerally.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include detectability/content-unawareness subnodes.

title: Users may be unaware that backend processing of motion alerts reveals occupancy behavior
description: If the system does not clearly communicate how real-time motion alerts are processed, retained, or analyzed by the backend, users may not understand that their household activity patterns can be observed or inferred from these alerts.
assumptions: Assumes privacy notices or in-product explanations do not fully explain backend-side processing and implications of motion-alert forwarding.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include unawareness subnodes.

title: Backend receipt and use of motion alerts may exceed the user's consent or choice
description: If users have not specifically agreed to backend forwarding, retention, analytics, or secondary use of motion alerts, the destination's processing may go beyond the scope of their consent or configured privacy choices.
assumptions: Assumes consent/granular privacy controls for motion-alert sharing or downstream use may be absent, bundled, or insufficiently specific.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include non-compliance subnodes.

title: Notification content may disclose in-home activity beyond necessity
description: By pushing a motion-detected alert to the homeowner, the backend shares occupancy/activity information. If the notification includes detailed content such as exact timestamps, room/camera identifiers, thumbnails, or repeated event details, it may disclose more about household behavior than is necessary for the alerting purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the push notification may contain event details rather than a minimal generic alert.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on generic disclosure-at-source reasoning; exact LINDDUN Pro subnode may differ.

title: Push-notification metadata can link homeowner, device, and home activity
description: Even if notification payloads are protected, metadata on the flow such as recipient push token, timing, frequency, and correlation with motion events can allow linking a specific homeowner/device to a particular home and its activity patterns.
assumptions: Assumes standard mobile push infrastructure exposes or processes delivery metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode may vary; threat is grounded in linkability via communication metadata in transit.

title: Notification traffic may identify the homeowner or household as a monitored residence
description: The existence and routing metadata of motion-alert notifications can identify the recipient device/account as belonging to a home-security user, and potentially to a specific household, especially when combined with provider or network-side information.
assumptions: Assumes intermediaries or observers can access push-service metadata or infer service usage from traffic patterns.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort tree-node selection; identification may depend on the push architecture and observability of metadata.

title: Notification contents or metadata may be exposed in transit or via push intermediaries
description: Motion-detected notifications commonly traverse third-party push services and networks. If payloads are not minimized or protected, intermediaries or eavesdroppers may learn sensitive facts such as that motion occurred, when it occurred, and possibly where.
assumptions: Assumes use of platform push services and that either payload or meaningful metadata is visible to intermediaries.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; disclosure through intermediaries is the core concern.

title: Notification preview on the phone may disclose home activity to bystanders
description: When the homeowner's device receives the alert, lock-screen previews, wearable mirroring, shared-device use, or notification history can expose motion events to nearby people or other device users who were not intended recipients.
assumptions: Assumes notifications may be shown on lock screen or synced to companion devices by default.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; this is a destination-side disclosure caused by device presentation/handling.

title: Frequent motion alerts enable profiling of household routines
description: On receipt, the homeowner's phone accumulates a history of motion notifications. This history can reveal occupancy schedules, sleep/work patterns, travel periods, and other behavioral routines if viewed by apps, device users, or anyone with access to the device.
assumptions: Assumes notifications are retained in notification history, backups, or companion-device logs.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort node id; threat is detectability/unawareness-style exposure of behavioral patterns from received alerts.

title: Homeowner may not have meaningful control over motion-alert content and timing
description: If the backend sends motion notifications without granular settings for sensitivity, quiet hours, content detail, or per-device delivery, the homeowner may lack sufficient control over how their household activity data is communicated.
assumptions: Assumes limited user-configurable notification/privacy settings.
uncertainty_note: Included as a plausible non-compliance/control issue for this flow; applicability depends on product settings and consent design.

title: Backend shares analytics that may still be linkable to users or devices
description: Although described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend's act of disclosing analytics to the vendor can enable linking of records to the same user, device, household, or account if aggregation is coarse, stable identifiers are retained, or small cohorts are shared.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics may contain persistent device/account identifiers, quasi-identifiers, or sufficiently granular segments despite being called aggregated.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types but not detailed node mappings for this specific case.

title: Aggregated analytics may still permit inference of individual behavior
description: The backend may disclose statistics, event counts, or segmented usage patterns from which the vendor can infer sensitive traits or behaviors about individual users or small groups, especially where aggregation buckets are small or repeatedly reported over time.
assumptions: Assumes analytics are segmented by dimensions such as region, app version, device model, or time window that can narrow groups substantially.
uncertainty_note: Inference risk depends strongly on aggregation thresholds and release frequency.

title: Analytics flow may disclose information in transit if insufficiently protected
description: If the transfer channel to the cloud analytics vendor is not strongly protected, the analytics payload could be observed by intermediaries, exposing usage information and potentially sensitive operational or behavioral data.
assumptions: Assumes transport security, endpoint authentication, or encryption at rest during transfer may be misconfigured or incomplete.
uncertainty_note: Applies as a generic in-transit disclosure threat; actual likelihood depends on implemented transport protections.

title: Vendor can link received analytics with other datasets
description: Upon receipt, the cloud analytics vendor may combine the analytics with other customer data, SDK telemetry, IP/device metadata, or its own datasets, enabling cross-context linkage of users, devices, or cohorts beyond the original purpose of aggregation.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor has access to additional datasets or metadata that make linkage feasible.
uncertainty_note: Exact linkage capability depends on the vendor's platform design and contractual restrictions.

title: Vendor may infer sensitive attributes from analytics
description: The vendor may analyze the received usage analytics to infer user interests, routines, demographics, or other sensitive characteristics, even if direct identifiers are absent.
assumptions: Assumes analytics dimensions and historical patterns are rich enough to support profiling or model-based inference.
uncertainty_note: Inference strength depends on data granularity and the vendor's enrichment capabilities.

title: Vendor may use analytics for secondary purposes beyond the original expectation
description: The cloud analytics vendor may retain, mine, or repurpose the analytics for service improvement, benchmarking, advertising, model training, or other secondary uses that exceed what users reasonably expect from app analytics processing.
assumptions: Assumes contractual terms or technical controls do not strictly limit downstream use.
uncertainty_note: This is a common downstream-use risk for third-party analytics, but actual applicability depends on the vendor agreement and configuration.

title: Sharing with a third-party analytics vendor may be insufficiently transparent to users
description: Users may be unaware that their app-usage data, even in aggregated form, is shared with an external analytics vendor, reducing transparency about recipients, purposes, retention, and downstream processing.
assumptions: Assumes privacy notices, in-app disclosures, or consent flows do not clearly explain this sharing.
uncertainty_note: Transparency depends on the application's notice and consent design.

title: Third-party analytics sharing may occur without a valid legal basis or honoring user choices
description: Sending analytics to the vendor may be non-compliant if the app lacks a valid legal basis, fails to obtain required consent for analytics/tracking, ignores opt-out signals, or transfers data contrary to contractual or jurisdictional restrictions.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics data is subject to privacy regulation and that consent/opt-out or transfer restrictions may apply.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations vary by jurisdiction and by whether the analytics is truly anonymized versus personal data.

title: Linkability via retrieval metadata on the video-fetch flow
description: The retrieval flow can expose stable identifiers or correlatable metadata such as homeowner account ID, device ID, camera ID, clip ID, timestamps, IP address, and access patterns. Observers of the flow or intermediaries with access to transport metadata may link multiple playback requests to the same household, device, or camera over time.
assumptions: Assumes the request/response path or associated logs expose persistent identifiers or rich metadata beyond what is strictly necessary, and that such metadata is observable by network infrastructure or service operators.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the specific Linkability subtree for this interaction.

title: Identifiability of the homeowner from video retrieval traffic
description: Even if the clip payload is protected, the act of retrieving a specific stored video may reveal the identity of the homeowner or household through account identifiers, authenticated session tokens, IP address, or uniquely identifying request patterns on this flow.
assumptions: Assumes identifiers or quasi-identifiers are present in transit metadata, headers, URLs, or operational logs associated with the flow.
uncertainty_note: Specific Identifiability tree-node id is an informed approximation; exact subtree was not present in the retrieved snippets.

title: Backend learns sensitive inferences from requested video clips
description: By retrieving and processing stored clips for playback, the mobile app backend can infer sensitive information about the homeowner's behavior, routines, occupancy, visitors, and events captured in the video. These inferences may go beyond what is necessary to serve playback.
assumptions: Assumes the backend can inspect clip content or detailed metadata and that internal use is broader than strict delivery for playback.
uncertainty_note: Threat applies if backend-side processing or analytics occur; if P2 only streams encrypted blobs without inspection, applicability is reduced. Tree-node citation is approximate.

title: Backend retrieves more video data than necessary for playback
description: The backend may fetch full-resolution clips, extended time ranges, or associated metadata not required for the homeowner's immediate playback request. This creates a detectability/disclosure risk by unnecessarily exposing additional personal data within P2.
assumptions: Assumes retrieval is not minimized to the exact clip segment, quality level, and metadata needed for the requested playback.
uncertainty_note: Exact Dd subtree may differ depending on the project's threat-tree version; applicability is strongest where minimization controls are weak.

title: Homeowner may be unaware that backend accesses stored clips for playback
description: If the architecture or notices do not make clear that the backend retrieves and potentially processes stored video before delivery, the data subject may lack awareness of this handling step and its privacy implications.
assumptions: Assumes transparency notices or UI explanations do not clearly describe backend-side retrieval and processing of stored clips.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the Unawareness subtree.

title: Retrieved video may be retained by the backend longer than necessary
description: After retrieving the stored clip from cloud video storage, the backend may cache, log, or otherwise retain the video or derived metadata longer than needed to fulfill playback. This would violate storage-limitation obligations.
assumptions: Assumes P2 stores temporary copies, caches, debug artifacts, or access logs containing personal data without strict retention limits.
